readings: The Son is superior to the angels
2027-03-22.alt: Hasha Week (Holy Week), the last week of the Great Fast. From today until the end of the season of the Dedication of the Church, the Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Order of the first Qudasha (of Mar Addai and Mari), as the calendar notes.
2027-03-22.verse: and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.
theo: The Hosanna is over, and the week the St Thomas Christians call Hasha has begun. Hasha is the Syriac word for suffering: this is the week of the Lord's Passion, the last and holiest week of the Great Fast. From today, the calendar notes, the Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Order of the first Qudasha, the anaphora of Mar Addai and Mari, until the end of the season of the Dedication of the Church. Kerala homes keep the week with a rhythm of their own. The tender palm leaves (kuruthola) blessed yesterday are put away carefully, because on Thursday a small cross made from them will crown the Pesaha appam. Houses are cleaned, the last Lenten confessions are made, and in many parishes the forty hours' adoration brings families to the church by turns, day and night, while pilgrims keep climbing Malayattoor. The Church opens this week with a story from the first family of Israel: the beloved son sent by his father to his brothers. “Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his children” (Genesis 37:3). Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow to his sheaf, and then that “the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” His brothers ask, “Are you indeed to reign over us?” “So his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.” Then Jacob sends him: “Come, I will send you to them.” He answered, “Here I am.” Joseph wanders in the fields until a stranger asks him, “What are you seeking?” and he answers, “I am seeking my brothers.” They see him from far off and say, “Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits”. Only Reuben pleads, “Let us not take his life.” From the earliest centuries the Fathers saw in Joseph a picture of Christ: the beloved Son, sent by the Father, who comes looking for his brothers, and whom they plot to destroy. The whole of Hasha week answers the stranger's question in the field. What is he seeking? He is seeking his brothers and sisters. He is seeking us.

The second reading tells of a quarrel that almost became a civil war. The tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, settled east of the Jordan, build a great altar by the river. The other tribes take it for rebellion, a rival altar, and gather to fight. The eastern tribes answer with a cry: “The LORD, God of gods! The LORD, God of gods! He knows; and let Israel itself know!” They did not build it for sacrifice, they explain, but so that in time to come no one could tell their children, “You have no portion in the LORD.” It was to be “a witness between us and you”, and they swear: “Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD”. A misunderstanding between brothers is healed because both sides stopped to listen before they struck. Holy Week asks the same of us: one altar, one Lord, one people. No family quarrel and no parish faction should still be standing on Pesaha evening, when the whole parish gathers at one altar for one Qurbana. The Epistle lifts our eyes to the One who will walk the way of the Cross this week. The letter to the Hebrews gathers the psalms to show that the Son is above every angel: “For to which of the angels did God ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” When he comes into the world, “Let all God's angels worship him.” To the Son God says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever”. Heaven and earth “will perish, but you remain”, and “your years will never end.” The prisoner who will be bound on Thursday night, mocked on Friday and laid in a tomb is the eternal Son. That is why the Passion is not only a sad story: it is God himself who suffers in the flesh for us.

The Gospel takes us into the council that met after the raising of Lazarus. The chief priests and the Pharisees are afraid: “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and destroy both our holy place and our nation.” They lived under a foreign power that could crush a city for a single riot. Caiaphas, high priest that year, speaks with the cold arithmetic of power: “it is better for you to have one man die for the people than to have the whole nation destroyed.” John sees in these words a prophecy deeper than Caiaphas knew: Jesus was about to die for the nation, “and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.” We must read this carefully, as the Church does. The decision was taken by a few leaders in a frightened hour. The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597), and that all sinners were the authors of Christ's sufferings (Catechism 598). The question of this week is not who killed Jesus long ago, but whose sins he carried; and the answer is ours. Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness. In Jerusalem the pilgrims who have come early to purify themselves for the Passover ask one another in the temple, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival, will he?” He will come. He will come on purpose, to be the one man who dies for the people, so that the scattered children of God, from Jerusalem to Kerala and to every land where our people now live, may be gathered into one.
conn: The Syriac word for suffering. The St Thomas Christians call Holy Week the Hasha week, the week of the Lord's Passion.
The beloved son sent by his father, hated by his brothers, sold, and raised up to save them: Stephen tells this story to the council (Acts 7:9–10), and the Fathers read it as a figure of Christ.
Joseph's answer echoes Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8), and the Son's own word on entering the world: I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:7).
The eastern tribes named their altar Witness, “a witness between us that the LORD is God” (Joshua 22:34).
Hebrews 1:5–13 weaves Psalm 2:7, 2 Samuel 7:14, Psalm 45:6–7, Psalm 102:25–27 and Psalm 110:1 into one portrait of the Son.
Caiaphas speaks of one man dying for the people; Jesus had said that he lays down his life for the sheep and has other sheep to gather into one flock (John 10:15–16).
outline: Ask: what am I seeking this week, and do I know that the Son is seeking me?
The beloved son sent to his brothers.
The eternal Son goes to the Cross.
Point 4 · One man for the people
To gather the dispersed children of God.
“to gather into one the dispersed children of God.”
live: Begin each morning of Hasha week with Joseph's words, and do the first duty of the day willingly.
Before Pesaha, go and listen to someone you have misunderstood or who has misunderstood you, and be reconciled.
Keep yesterday's blessed palm safely for the Pesaha appam, and pray before it as a family tonight.
Take your turn at the forty hours' adoration, or make a visit to the Blessed Sacrament this week.
fathers: In holy Joseph we see Christ: sent by his father to his brothers, stripped of his robe, sold for silver, and afterwards the saviour of those who sold him. The brothers meant to put an end to his dreams, and by their very hatred the dream came true.

Caiaphas spoke the truth without knowing it. A wicked man uttered a prophecy, not by his own holiness but because of the office he held, for Christ was indeed to die to gather the scattered children of God into one.
magis: The religious authorities in Jerusalem were not unanimous about Jesus; the council's decision was taken in fear for the holy place and the nation.
The responsibility for the trial of Jesus cannot be ascribed to the Jews in Jerusalem as a whole, nor extended to the Jews of other times and places (Nostra Aetate 4).
Sinners themselves were the authors and ministers of all the sufferings that Christ endured.
Easter is the feast of feasts; Holy Week leads the Church to it.
2027-03-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, beloved Son of the Father, you came looking for your brothers and sisters, and you answered the Father, Here I am. In this Hasha week gather us, scattered by our sins and quarrels, into one family around your one altar. You are the eternal Son, whom the angels worship, and you chose to die for the people: let us not stand far off, but follow you to the Cross and to the joy of your Resurrection. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The council said one man must die for the people. At every Holy Qurbana that one death is made present on the altar, and the scattered children of God are gathered into one body.
Joseph went looking for his brothers in the fields; in the Qurbana the Son comes looking for us, and we answer as Joseph did: Here I am.

quick: Joseph, the beloved son, is sent by his father to his brothers, and they plot against him.
The tribes avoid a war by listening: one altar, one Lord, one people.
Caiaphas speaks better than he knows: Jesus will die to gather the scattered children of God.
2027-03-22.action: Before Pesaha, take the first step to heal one quarrel.
2027-03-22.question: Am I among those who plot, those who stand far off, or those the Son has gathered?
term: The Syriac word for suffering. The Syro-Malabar Church calls Holy Week the Hasha week, from Hosanna Sunday to Easter.

family.explain: Jacob loved his son Joseph very much. One day he sent Joseph to find his brothers, who were looking after the sheep far away. Joseph said: Here I am. But his brothers were jealous, and when they saw him coming they planned to hurt him. Jesus is like Joseph: God the Father sent him to us, his brothers and sisters, even though he knew some would not welcome him.
family.intention: We pray for families who are divided by quarrels, that they may be reconciled before Easter.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there anyone in our family or among our neighbours we need to make peace with this week?”

illus: Two brothers near Thodupuzha had not spoken for eleven years, all because of a boundary wall between their houses. Each blamed the other, and their children grew up as strangers. In Holy Week the parish kept the forty hours' adoration, and the younger brother signed up for the hour after midnight because he could not sleep. When he came in, he found his elder brother already kneeling in the front row. They prayed the hour side by side without a word. Outside, under the street light, the elder one said only: Come home on Thursday. On Pesaha evening the two families broke the appam at one table.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you came looking for your brothers and sisters. Find us now, and gather us into one. Amen.
share: Come, I will send you to them (Genesis 37:13). Where is God sending me this week, and do I answer, Here I am?
Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD (Joshua 22:29). Is there a misunderstanding I need to listen to before I judge?
to gather into one the dispersed children of God (John 11:52). Who is scattered from our family, parish or group, and how can I help bring them home?
interc: For the Church in Hasha week, that she may walk with Christ to the Cross.
For families and parishes divided by quarrels, that they may be reconciled before Pesaha.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, and for friendship between Christians and Jews.
For pilgrims at Malayattoor and all who keep the forty hours' adoration.
For our group, that we may answer the Father as Joseph did: Here I am.
pm.close: Father, you sent your beloved Son to look for his brothers and sisters, and he gave his life to gather your scattered children. Heal our divisions and keep us faithful this holy week. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Hosanna is over and the Hasha week has begun, the week of the Lord's suffering. The Church opens it with Joseph, the beloved son whom his father sends to his brothers: come, I will send you to them; and Joseph answers, here I am (Genesis 37:13).

His brothers see him coming and say: here comes this dreamer; come now, let us kill him (Genesis 37:19–20). The Fathers saw Christ in Joseph. The Father sends his beloved Son to us, his brothers and sisters, knowing that he will be rejected. He comes anyway. He is seeking us.

The tribes of Israel almost go to war over an altar by the Jordan, but they stop and listen, and the quarrel is healed. This week the whole parish will gather at one altar on Pesaha evening. Let no quarrel in our family or parish still be standing then.

Hebrews tells us who it is that suffers this week: the Son whom all God's angels worship, whose throne is forever and ever (Hebrews 1:6, 8). The one who is bound, mocked and crucified is the eternal Son of God.

In the council Caiaphas says it is better for one man to die for the people. John tells us that Jesus died not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God (John 11:52). Not one people against another, but all our sins put him on the Cross, and his love gathers us all. Let us go up with him to Jerusalem this week. Amen.
kids: Children, Joseph's father sent him to find his brothers, and Joseph said: Here I am! God the Father sent Jesus to find us. This week, when someone calls you, can you answer happily: Here I am?

intro: Theme: “and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.”
The beloved son sent to his brothers, an altar of witness, the eternal Son above the angels, and the one man who dies for the people.

q: And Israel said to Joseph, “Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them.” He answered, “Here I am.”
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him,
points.apply: Begin each morning of Hasha week by saying to the Father: Here I am.

q: How very good and pleasant it is when kindred live together in unity!
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
points.apply: Go and listen to one person you have quarrelled with, before Pesaha evening.

sub: A prophecy deeper than Caiaphas knew.
q: But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.

He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.
points.apply: Pray this week for someone who has drifted away from the Church, and invite them to the Pesaha Qurbana.

concl: The Father sends his beloved Son to look for his brothers and sisters, and the Son goes willingly to die for the people.
Let us stop quarrelling, gather at one altar, and let him gather us into one.
2027-03-22.resolve: Heal one quarrel and invite one scattered person home before Pesaha.
